author.name: Aeschylus
author.biography: Aeschylus fought in the Persian Wars and wrote for Athens's civic and religious theatre. His audience encountered old myths while living through the construction of a powerful, contested public world. The Oresteia brings those scales together. A wounded household demands repayment in blood; a city must find some way to stop the repayment. The question of justice becomes the question of how people can continue to live together.

hook.text: Who gets to end a cycle of revenge?

paragraphs: A king is coming home from war. His return should restore a household. The household has been waiting with injuries of its own.

Across three plays, Aeschylus lets one demand for justice become the cause of the next. Each act can be explained by a previous wrong. The explanation does not erase the new suffering it creates. A child may inherit a duty to avenge a parent without having chosen the world that makes the duty seem necessary.

The trilogy asks how people could ever leave such a pattern. Who can judge when every participant has a claim? What must a community build if punishment is to become something other than the next family's grievance?

Listen to the voices that insist their pain cannot simply be set aside. A stable settlement may need authority, persuasion and concessions that nobody finds entirely satisfying. When does accepting an imperfect judgment become more courageous than pursuing the justice you know you deserve?

orientation.text: Read Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers and The Eumenides in sequence. The household's earlier history is gradually disclosed by speeches and the chorus.
